reason: The transporter-bearing cell and incoming glucose and oxygen suggest the first step toward making usable energy.
expectation: The cell will take in fuel for energy production.

effect: The transporter-bearing cell forms the muscle fibre scaffold with the fibre structures; fuel must be handled another way.
reaction: I was surprised that the attempted fuel combination instead assembled the scaffold.
reason: Glucose and oxygen are inputs for energy production, and mitochondria are associated with that process.
expectation: The mitochondria will use the fuel and oxygen in a step toward producing usable energy.

effect: The fuelled mitochondria are ready for the next energy-production step; the picture also shows glucose being split in the cell fluid first.
reaction: The picture clarified where the initial fuel processing happens.
reason: ADP and phosphate are the available ingredients for making ATP.
expectation: The fuelled mitochondria will help make ATP from ADP and phosphate.

effect: The ATP supply is available for the muscle’s pulling machinery, and the picture shows ADP and phosphate returning to be reused.
reaction: The cycle makes the continuing energy supply clearer.
reason: Thin actin filaments and thick myosin filaments are the complementary parts of the pulling machinery.
expectation: The filaments will form a contractile unit for the muscle fibre.

effect: The actin and myosin filaments form sliding filament units that can be added to the muscle fibre.
reaction: The overlapping arrangement fits the idea of a pulling mechanism.
reason: The muscle fibre scaffold has spaces for its contractile units.
expectation: The sliding filament units will become part of the muscle fibre.

effect: The sliding filament units are now installed in the muscle fibre, preparing it for the pulling mechanism.
reaction: It is satisfying to see the separate filaments become part of the fibre.
reason: The fibre has its pulling machinery, and the ATP supply was shown serving that machinery.
expectation: The ATP supply will enable a step toward muscle pulling.

effect: ATP prepares the myosin heads to release and reset, but the binding sites remain covered.
reaction: The close-up makes ATP’s role more specific than simply supplying energy.
reason: The calcium signal is the remaining cue associated with the fibre’s filaments and may uncover the binding sites.
expectation: Calcium will allow the filaments to interact and the fibre to pull.

effect: Calcium exposes the grip sites, allowing myosin to pull the filaments past each other; the filaments themselves do not shorten.
reaction: The distinction between the fibre shortening and the filaments sliding is clear and interesting.
reason: The remaining calcium-pumping membranes can return calcium to storage, which should let the fibre relax.
expectation: Calcium will be pumped back into storage, allowing the muscle fibre to relax.

effect: The calcium pumps return calcium to storage using ATP, covering the grip sites again and stopping the pull. The fibre is then ready to respond again.
reaction: I found it interesting that relaxation also requires cellular work.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the calcium signal was most worthwhile: the description connects the signal to exposed grip sites, myosin pulling and the fibre shortening while the filaments slide.

leastWorthwhile.text: Assembling the fibre scaffold was less clear than the later steps. My attempted fuel combination led automatically to the scaffold, so I did not see why those two pieces belonged together beforehand.

surprise.text: I was surprised that relaxation needs ATP-powered pumps to return calcium to storage.

arbitrary.text: The scaffold combination initially felt somewhat arbitrary because the connection between the transporter-bearing cell and the fibre structures was not obvious to me from their titles alone.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the sequence made me curious how a working muscle fibre connects to tissues and larger body systems.
